final_answer: Inflammation dilutes and depolymerizes synovial HA (ROS and hyaluronidases), so both concentration and MW drop, reducing lubrication and promoting further inflammatory signaling from fragments.
note: Evidence PMC9797074 supports decreased HA molecular weight and increased HA fragments in osteoarthritic synovial fluid versus healthy high-MW HA, but no window states that HA concentration/amount falls in inflamed joints, or that ROS/hyaluronidases cause the depolymerization, so the amount and mechanism claims are unsettled.

final_answer: Fragments are generated specifically by tissue damage and are absent from intact tissue; they alert innate immunity (TLR2/4, CD44) that injury occurred - the definition of a damage-associated molecular pattern.
note: Evidence PMC5373089 defines DAMPs as released after tissue injury and activating innate immunity via toll-like receptors; PMC5760314 shows TLR2 and CD44 mediate macrophage responses to DAMPs present in OA synovial fluid.

final_answer: Early wounds are rich in fragments (pro-inflammatory, pro-angiogenic signals that recruit cells); resolution requires clearance of fragments and restoration of HMW-HA, and failure to switch is linked to chronic wounds/fibrosis.
note: No window describes a time course of HA fragments versus HMW-HA in wounds, fragment clearance and HMW-HA restoration, or a link between failure to switch and chronic wounds/fibrosis; windows cover diabetic wound immune dysfunction, HA-iodine wound treatment, and HMW-HA tube formation only.

final_answer: Dense HMW-HA gel swells with water, raises interstitial pressure, collapses microvessels, and creates a diffusion barrier - limiting drug and immune-cell access independent of any signaling effect.
note: Evidence PMC6764447 states collagen and hyaluronan overexpression contributes to a protective tumor microenvironment by supporting high interstitial fluid pressure and creating a tortuous setting for convection and diffusion of chemotherapeutic molecules; PMC11706246 describes high interstitial fluid pressure and a dense ECM barrier hindering intratumor drug distribution.

final_answer: B - HAS2 overexpression raises synthesis; the others increase degradation or clearance.
note: Evidence PMC4758074 states miR-23a-3p decreases HAS2-mediated HA content and HAS2 is a target gene of miR-23a-3p, supporting HAS2 overexpression (option B) as the synthesis-increasing change.

final_answer: Removing their very-HMW-HA made the cells susceptible to malignant transformation, demonstrating causality of HMW-HA in their cancer resistance.
note: Evidence PMC3720720 states that once high molecular weight HA is removed by either knocking down HAS2 or overexpressing the HA-degrading enzyme Hyal2, naked mole-rat cells become susceptible to malignant transformation and readily form tumors in mice.

final_answer: Serum HA is misleading because, as one of the four liver-fibrosis markers, it is sensitive but poorly specific: those markers also increase in renal fibrosis, pulmonary fibrosis and other organ fibrosis, and are also affected by bone growth, drugs, etc.
note: Draft's joint-inflammation and renal-impairment examples are not in the evidence; the decisive fragments are: "The four items of liver fiber not only increase in liver fibrosis, but also in renal fibrosis, pulmonary fibrosis and other organ fibrosis" and they are "affected by bone growth, drugs, etc.", with "the disadvantages of high sensitivity and poor specificity" (PMC9843355).

final_answer: The evidence does not support a fragment-pro-angiogenic versus HMW-HA-anti-angiogenic dichotomy: HMW-HA itself was reported to increase angiogenesis by promoting endothelial cell proliferation, migration and tube formation, and HA-CD44 signaling is linked to tumor progression and angiogenesis, while the exact mechanisms by which HA contributes to tumor angiogenesis are not yet well elucidated.
note: The decisive fragments are: "HMW-HA increases endothelial cell proliferation, migration and tube formation" (PMC5823590) and "The exact mechanisms by which HA can contribute with tumor angiogenesis has not yet been well elucidated" (PMC4685440); no window supports oligosaccharide-driven angiogenesis or an anti-angiogenic HMW-HA.

final_answer: The gel liquefies (syneresis) as HA depolymerizes/redistributes and collagen aggregates, leading to floaters and posterior vitreous detachment.
note: Evidence PMC6305337 states the vitreous liquefies with age, resulting in phase-separation and gel network collapse, and causing complications including vitreous floaters; PMC10981431 states the age-related loss of hyaluronic acid primarily drives straylight from conglomerates of collagen and that posterior vitreous detachment is present in 65% of patients >65 years and is the most common etiology of floaters.

final_answer: Perineuronal nets: HA backbones organize lecticans (CSPGs) and link proteins around neurons, gating synaptic plasticity.
note: Evidence PMC5347017 states hyaluronan can form the backbone of specialised lattice-like extracellular matrix structures termed perineuronal nets, which surround mature GABAergic interneurons and are associated with synaptic stability and plasticity; PMC10705503 states HAPLN link proteins link CSPGs to HA.

final_answer: Marked HA accumulation in edematous alveolar exudates (with upregulated HAS and downregulated degradation reported), proposed to contribute to the gel-like lung fluid - a finding still being mechanistically debated.
note: Evidence PMC7650240 states inflammatory cytokines (IL-1 beta, IL-6, TNF alpha) are strong inducers of HAS2 and that hyperinflammation induces the production and accumulation of HA within the alveolar spaces, reporting abundant HA in the lungs of patients deceased with severe Covid-19; PMC11633090 reports fragmented HA accumulates in the lungs of COVID-19 patients.

final_answer: Skin HA turns over in under a day, while cartilage HA (locked in aggregates) persists for weeks - turnover is set by local drainage, receptor clearance, and matrix entrapment.
note: No window gives HA turnover times for skin (under a day) or cartilage (weeks), or discusses drainage, receptor clearance or matrix entrapment; windows cover skin laxity, collagen turnover, skin density and skin gene-expression biomarkers only.

final_answer: Estrogen supports dermal HA content; its postmenopausal fall parallels skin HA loss, dryness, and thinning.
note: Evidence shows estrogen affects skin regulation and ER-beta scaffolds aid skin repair, and that aging reduces hyaluronan-mediated water retention, but no window states estrogen supports dermal HA content or that the postmenopausal estrogen fall causes dermal HA loss, dryness and thinning, so the draft's causal chain is unsettled.

final_answer: Physiological loading stimulates chondrocyte HA (and aggrecan) synthesis, maintaining the aggregate pool; overload/unloading disturbs this balance toward catabolism.
note: No window states physiological loading stimulates chondrocyte HA (or aggrecan) synthesis or contrasts overload/unloading; windows cover cytokine-driven aggrecan catabolism in OA, hydrodynamic friction/permeability of aggrecan, and GAG loss reducing cartilage compressive stiffness.

final_answer: HA accumulates in the renal interstitium (driven by hyperglycemia and inflammation), where it is associated with leukocyte infiltration and fibrosis progression.
note: Evidence does not state HA accumulates in the diabetic renal interstitium with leukocyte infiltration and fibrosis progression; PMC4816883 only says elevated HYAL activity in the diabetic kidney may contribute to the inability to gain sufficient elevation in interstitial HA during hydration, which does not settle (and partly cuts against) the accumulation claim, and the remaining windows concern lymphangiogenesis and renal fibrosis generally.

final_answer: Aging fibroblasts shift HAS/HYAL expression and produce less and shorter HA with a thinner pericellular coat, weakening HA-dependent signaling and hydration in aged dermis.
note: No window discusses senescent/aging fibroblasts, age-related HAS/HYAL expression shifts, production of less/shorter HA, or a thinner pericellular coat; windows cover Hyal-2/WWOX/Smad4 signaling in cancer cells, HYAL for filler dissolution, and HYAL effects on normal human dermal fibroblasts.

final_answer: HA rises early in injured tissue, HAS2 overexpression alone can drive fibrotic phenotypes in models, and blocking HA synthesis (4-MU) attenuates fibrosis - supporting a causal, not merely reactive, role.
note: No window shows HA rising early in injured tissue before fibrosis, HAS2 overexpression driving fibrotic phenotypes, or blocking HA synthesis with 4-MU attenuating fibrosis; windows cover HAS2-AS1 in ovulation/cumulus expansion, lymphangiogenesis correlations in fibrosis, and a HAS2 overexpression vector in porcine granulosa cells.

final_answer: Fetal wounds heal scarlessly in an HA-rich environment with prolonged HMW-HA presence, a contrast with adult wounds where HA is rapidly fragmented - one rationale for HA-based scar-modulating products.
note: Evidence supports scarless mid-gestation fetal wound healing and an IL-10-linked large HA-rich pericellular matrix (PMC3959980), but no window mentions HA in amniotic fluid, prolonged HMW-HA presence, or rapid HA fragmentation in adult wounds, so the draft's specific HA claims are unsettled.

final_answer: The glucuronic-acid carboxyl group, typically via carbodiimide coupling (EDC/NHS) to form amides with amine-bearing molecules.
note: Evidence PMC5527969 states the carboxyl group of HA is derivatized to an amide via carbodiimide-based activation with EDC and NHS followed by reaction with an amine; PMC8466770 states HA is mainly modified through its carboxyl group affording amide formation using carbodiimide derivatives such as EDC along with NHS.

final_answer: By reacting HA hydroxyl groups with methacrylic anhydride (typically at controlled pH), grafting methacrylate groups that later photopolymerize with a photoinitiator.
note: Evidence PMC10959719 gives a protocol to prepare hyaluronic acid methacrylate utilizing sodium hyaluronate, methacrylic anhydride and 5 M NaOH solution; PMC11904389 states HA-MA was synthesized using methacrylic anhydride under basic conditions; PMC5460858 describes photo-crosslinkable methacrylated HA (MeHA) hydrogels whose moduli increase on UV irradiation.
